messages.subject: over-ride fileInput maximum size
messages.body_plain:
Hi guys,

I'm new to shiny, so pardon the relatively simple question.

I'm using Shiny to create a GUI for users to run some analysis. However, they are required to input a few files through different fileInput, and yet each of the file is in the excess of 100MB. The maximum, as I understand, is 5MB per file. Is there any way to override this maximum? I read that it can be done using the following:

option(shiny.maxRequestSize = -1)

However, I'm not too sure where do I place this code? Do I place it inside the Shiny server codes, or is there another config file that I need to create?

Sorry for the trivial question, and thanks!

Jeremy

messages.subject: Re: Error: su: must be run from a terminal
messages.subject_clean: Error: su: must be run from a terminal
messages.body_plain:
This is essentially the change you need:
https://github.com/jcheng5/shiny-server/tree/no-su

Sorry for the delay in properly finishing and integrating this patch. The good news is that we've decided this should be the "default" way that Shiny Server should be deployed (single non-root user owning both the Shiny Server process and the spawned R processes). I'm a little backed up right now but hopefully by the next Shiny Server release you will be able to make this work right out of the box; but in the meantime you can install from that branch if you want to.

On Tue, Apr 30, 2013 at 6:32 PM, Tristan Sloughter <tristan....@gmail.com> wrote:
> Any movement on this? I may have to try digging into it if not. If so any pointers would be great :)
>
>
> On Sat, Apr 20, 2013 at 11:52 AM, Tristan Sloughter <tristan....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Ah ok.
> >
> > That would be great if you could take care of allowing it to run as non-root. I'm using Shiny at Heroku, so want to be able to run it on our infrastructure :)
> >
> >
> > On Fri, Apr 19, 2013 at 4:37 PM, Joe Cheng <j...@rstudio.com> wrote:
> > > Despite the misleading error message, the problem here is indeed that Shiny Server expects to be run with root privileges.
> > >
> > > This is because Shiny Server was originally designed to allow all users (or all users in a certain group) on the server to host Shiny apps themselves, and their apps would execute with their permissions. We use su to drop privileges when spawning the R process (rather than simply fork/setuid/exec), since it knows all the subtleties about doing so, e.g. which environment variables need to be dropped/changed, the right incantation to setgid/initgroups, etc.
> > >
> > > Shiny Server still allows you to do this (it's the autouser <http://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://github.com/rstudio/shiny-server/blob/master/config.html#overview> mode) but with the other two modes of operation, "site directory" (the default) and "direct mapping", it's easy to imagine the Shiny Server process running as a particular user and all the spawned R processes running as the same user. Other than listening on port <1024 there would be no inherent need to run as root. But Shiny Server doesn't detect that case right now.
> > >
> > > I didn't think about the PaaS case--that is a particularly good reason for us to remove the run-as-root restriction. I'll see if I can take care of this.
> > >
> > >
> > > On Fri, Apr 19, 2013 at 12:35 PM, Tristan Sloughter <tristan....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > The real problem is that Heroku doesn't run the process with a tty.
> > > >
> > > > What is Shiny trying to do here? Why does it need a terminal?
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Fri, Apr 19, 2013 at 10:50 AM, Tristan Sloughter <tristan....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > And this is not possible on PaaS environments like Heroku.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Fri, Apr 19, 2013 at 10:47 AM, Jonathan Winters <jnw...@nyu.edu> wrote:
> > > > > > Dear Tristan,
> > > > > > I was able to get this running by loading the shiny-server using sudo as follows:
> > > > > > .
> > > > > > $ sudo shiny-server
> > > > > >
> > > > > > My hunch is that when you tell the system to load the shiny-server in the production environment you will want the "web server" to load automatically with administrative privileges. However, there may be a security issue with this?
> > > > > > Anyone with more advanced knowledge on this please chime in.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Regards,
> > > > > > Jonathan
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Friday, April 12, 2013 4:56:08 PM UTC-4, Tristan Sloughter wrote:
> > > > > > > I have a Shiny app that runs fine locally. I then took the Node.js and R Heroku buildpacks to deploy the app to Heroku. This mostly works, I have the app starting but when I load the page I get an odd error.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > In the logs I see:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > shiny-server - Error getting worker: Error: The application exited during initialization.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > And when I load the app in my browser I get:

> > > > > > > > An error has occurred

> > > > > > > Does anyone know what it is trying to do with 'su' to start a worker? And ideas why it would fail?
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Thanks,
> > > > > > > Tristan

messages.subject: Re: storing a dataframe
messages.body_plain:
Oh, that won't work at all. Try this instead:

shinyServer(function(input, output) {
  values <- reactiveValues(a=NULL)
  observe({
    values$a <- make.a.vector.or.dataframe.bases.on.wigdet.inputs()
  })
})

However, are you sure you don't want to just do it like this?

shinyServer(function(input, output) {
  # Define the vector or dataframe or whatever as a reactive expression
  myVector <- reactive({
    make.a.vector.or.dataframe.bases.on.wigdet.inputs()
  })

  # Use the reactive expression as if it's a function
  output$vectorPlot <- renderPlot({
    print(qplot(data=myVector(), ...))
  })
})

myVector will only be recalculated once each time the inputs change, even if you make many calls to it from your different renderXXX functions or other reactive expressions.

messages.subject: Re: ROAuth & twitteR package on Shiny Glimmer hosting--Completing the ROAuth handshake in a Shiny app
messages.subject_clean: ROAuth & twitteR package on Shiny Glimmer hosting--Completing the ROAuth handshake in a Shiny app
messages.body_plain:
Hey Eric—

I haven't tried this out yet, but it should work, in theory. In a regular R session (off server) do the following:

library(ROAuth)
library(RCurl)

requestURL <- "https://api.twitter.com/oauth/request_token"
accessURL <- "http://api.twitter.com/oauth/access_token"
authURL <- "http://api.twitter.com/oauth/authorize"
consumerKey <- "XXX"
consumerSecret <- "XXX"
my_oauth <- OAuthFactory$new(consumerKey=consumerKey,
  consumerSecret=consumerSecret, requestURL=requestURL,
  accessURL=accessURL, authURL=authURL)

## run this line and go to the URL that appears on screen
my_oauth$handshake(cainfo = system.file("CurlSSL", "cacert.pem", package = "RCurl"))

## Setting working folder
setwd("/your/path/")

## now you can save oauth token for use in future sessions with twitteR or streamR
save(my_oauth, file="my_oauth")

So if you load that "my_oauth" file into Shiny (on the server) you *should* be able to have OAuth authentification with:

load("my_oauth")
registerTwitterOAuth(my_oauth)

Good luck! Let me know if that works for you.

—M

messages.subject: Saving Shiny Rendered HTML
messages.body_plain:
My question is about how to save shiny rendered html pages. I am not sure this is the right forum to put this question, but I still wanted to try.

To give you some context, I just added a Shiny based app to rCharts, adapting the excellent Shiny app put together by @yihui for knitr. It allows users to embed d3js charts in an R Notebook. Here is a screencast for those interested, http://youtu.be/MqMkCk-nc6k,  but if you just want to see it in action, type this from your R console.

devtools::install_github('rCharts', 'ramnathv')
rCharts::open_notebook()

Now, I want to add a feature that allows a user to click on a publish button, that automatically publishes the source Rmd (from the text area) and the shiny rendered HTML to a github repo. I can generate static HTML independent of Shiny using Slidify, but I thought it would simplify the workflow considerably if a user can tweak the source using the notebook, and when happy with the end-product can hit publish.

This might be a question for the javascript community, but if any of you have thoughts on how to do this, I would appreciate it.

Best,
Ramnath

messages.subject: Re: best practise to reload data daily in server.R?
messages.subject_clean: best practise to reload data daily in server.R?
messages.body_plain:
Sorry for the delay in replying, your message got caught by the Google Groups spam filter.

We hope to make file monitoring much, much nicer in the future, but for now here's what you can do:

Let's say you have a function getLatestFile() that knows what directory to look in and how to identify the latest file. You could put this at the very top of your server.R (outside of shinyServer()):

values <- reactiveValues()
values$file <- getLatestFile()
observe({
  invalidateLater(10 * 60 * 1000)  # 10 minutes, in milliseconds
  values$file <- getLatestFile()
})

Then everywhere you need to refer to the filename, you will read from "values$file". The "observe" code block will execute every 10 minutes, and if values$file ever changes, then any reactive expressions/outputs that depend on its value will know they need to reexecute.

I don't know if there is an easy way to drop a dynamic header title into headerPanel, but if you can just have the date stamp shown somewhere else then it's easy, just use a textOutput along with renderText.

These are the possible solutions I can think of:

messages.subject: Re: Saving Shiny Rendered HTML
messages.body_plain:
Yes. I am only recommending it for local use. Can you elaborate on the firewall issue? How does it affect local use?

I had an idea for using the app only as a viewer, when online. In other words, the online version would load both *.Rmd and *.html in side-by-side windows just like Yihui's app, and will have all the features enabled, except that the knit button will be disabled. So a user can only view the source and the output online, NOT be able to run any code.

In addition, a download button on the top (similar to nbViewer) would allow users to download the Rmd, and a utility function will allow a user to recreate it locally using Shiny. I believe, this would entail the same risks as running runGitHub or runApp or sourcing any external script. I understand that the HTML can have malicious code as well, but I believe that possibility exists on any website that a user visits.

Let me know what you think, and if you have any ideas/suggestions.

Best,
Ramnath

messages.body_plain:
With local use and no firewall, anyone who can see your machine could point their browser to http://your-hostname:8100 and get access to the app.

Your viewer would work, just make sure that you don't merely disable the UI, but also conditionalize the server.R code so that the knitting can never happen. If you only disable the UI, it would still be possible for an attacker to make JavaScript calls that would simulate the clicking of the knit button or whatever. If you end up building this I can review the code for you.

messages.subject: Re: Saving Shiny Rendered HTML
messages.body_plain:
Let me understand this correctly. When I run any Shiny app on localhost:8100, it can be accessed by others? What steps can I take to ensure that this does not happen? I have been running all kinds of localhost applications, without being aware of this problem.

About the viewer, yes, that is what I had in mind. I will get rid of the server.R  code that does the knitting, completely, so that there is no way anyone can knit the Rmd file. All it would do is to load the Rmd file on the left pane and the HTML on the right pane, with links to download the source Rmd and the HTML. A utility function would then allow a user to load the Rmd file into a local shiny instance, and modify it and watch the HTML change.

Let me put a rough draft of this together and send you the code, so that you can review it and give me some feedback.

Best,
Ramnath

On Friday, May 3, 2013 12:41:13 PM UTC-6, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> With local use and no firewall, anyone who can see your machine could point their browser to http://your-hostname:8100 and get access to the app.
>
> Your viewer would work, just make sure that you don't merely disable the UI, but also conditionalize the server.R code so that the knitting can never happen. If you only disable the UI, it would still be possible for an attacker to make JavaScript calls that would simulate the clicking of the knit button or whatever. If you end up building this I can review the code for you.
>
>
> On Fri, May 3, 2013 at 12:19 AM, Ramnath Vaidyanathan <ramnath...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Yes. I am only recommending it for local use. Can you elaborate on the firewall issue? How does it affect local use?
> >
> > I had an idea for using the app only as a viewer, when online. In other words, the online version would load both *.Rmd and *.html in side-by-side windows just like Yihui's app, and will have all the features enabled, except that the knit button will be disabled. So a user can only view the source and the output online, NOT be able to run any code.
> >
> > In addition, a download button on the top (similar to nbViewer) would allow users to download the Rmd, and a utility function will allow a user to recreate it locally using Shiny. I believe, this would entail the same risks as running runGitHub or runApp or sourcing any external script. I understand that the HTML can have malicious code as well, but I believe that possibility exists on any website that a user visits.
> >
> > Let me know what you think, and if you have any ideas/suggestions.
> >
> > Best,
> > Ramnath
> >
> >
> >
> > On Thursday, May 2, 2013 11:18:00 PM UTC-4, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> > > The knitr Shiny app by Yihui was really cool but also a huge security hole--I hope you are only recommending it for local use and only when properly protected by a firewall!
> > >
> > >
> > > On Wed, May 1, 2013 at 3:58 PM, Ramnath Vaidyanathan <ramnath...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > My question is about how to save shiny rendered html pages. I am not sure this is the right forum to put this question, but I still wanted to try.
> > > >
> > > > To give you some context, I just added a Shiny based app to rCharts, adapting the excellent Shiny app put together by @yihui for knitr. It allows users to embed d3js charts in an R Notebook. Here is a screencast for those interested, http://youtu.be/MqMkCk-nc6k,  but if you just want to see it in action, type this from your R console.
> > > >
> > > > devtools::install_github('rCharts', 'ramnathv')
> > > > rCharts::open_notebook()
> > > >
> > > > Now, I want to add a feature that allows a user to click on a publish button, that automatically publishes the source Rmd (from the text area) and the shiny rendered HTML to a github repo. I can generate static HTML independent of Shiny using Slidify, but I thought it would simplify the workflow considerably if a user can tweak the source using the notebook, and when happy with the end-product can hit publish.
> > > >
> > > > This might be a question for the javascript community, but if any of you have thoughts on how to do this, I would appreciate it.
> > > >
> > > > Best,
> > > > Ramnath

messages.subject: access to shiny server
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am a green bird in Linux and web server. Recently I am trying to deploy a web application using R for my website. After some search on internet, I decided to use ubuntu 12.04 and shiny-server for setting up my website. I followed the instruction in the website https://github.com/rstudio/shiny-server, and it worked perfectly well until I tried to access it. I used the examples given in the website and I am able to access it via http://localhost:3838/examples/. My wlan0 inet addr is 192.168.10.103, and I can also access it via http://192.168.10.103:3838/examples/. But how can my friend access it? I tried to replace the wlan0 inet addr with my ip address and it does not work.
Thanks for you help!

Best,
Xu

messages.subject: Re: Saving Shiny Rendered HTML
messages.body_plain:
I am in the process of building the viewer. While building it, I realized that I can do it purely in Javascript, since there is no necessity for interaction with R, as we are going to be disabling any ability to run arbitrary code. I will put a working prototype on github soon, and can then make the call if there are advantages to hosting it on a Shiny server.

Ramnath

On Friday, May 3, 2013 3:38:53 PM UTC-4, Ramnath Vaidyanathan wrote:
> Let me understand this correctly. When I run any Shiny app on localhost:8100, it can be accessed by others? What steps can I take to ensure that this does not happen? I have been running all kinds of localhost applications, without being aware of this problem.
>
> About the viewer, yes, that is what I had in mind. I will get rid of the server.R  code that does the knitting, completely, so that there is no way anyone can knit the Rmd file. All it would do is to load the Rmd file on the left pane and the HTML on the right pane, with links to download the source Rmd and the HTML. A utility function would then allow a user to load the Rmd file into a local shiny instance, and modify it and watch the HTML change.
>
> Let me put a rough draft of this together and send you the code, so that you can review it and give me some feedback.
>
> Best,
> Ramnath
>
>
> On Friday, May 3, 2013 12:41:13 PM UTC-6, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> > With local use and no firewall, anyone who can see your machine could point their browser to http://your-hostname:8100 and get access to the app.
> >
> > Your viewer would work, just make sure that you don't merely disable the UI, but also conditionalize the server.R code so that the knitting can never happen. If you only disable the UI, it would still be possible for an attacker to make JavaScript calls that would simulate the clicking of the knit button or whatever. If you end up building this I can review the code for you.
> >
> >
> > On Fri, May 3, 2013 at 12:19 AM, Ramnath Vaidyanathan <ramnath...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Yes. I am only recommending it for local use. Can you elaborate on the firewall issue? How does it affect local use?
> > >
> > > I had an idea for using the app only as a viewer, when online. In other words, the online version would load both *.Rmd and *.html in side-by-side windows just like Yihui's app, and will have all the features enabled, except that the knit button will be disabled. So a user can only view the source and the output online, NOT be able to run any code.
> > >
> > > In addition, a download button on the top (similar to nbViewer) would allow users to download the Rmd, and a utility function will allow a user to recreate it locally using Shiny. I believe, this would entail the same risks as running runGitHub or runApp or sourcing any external script. I understand that the HTML can have malicious code as well, but I believe that possibility exists on any website that a user visits.
> > >
> > > Let me know what you think, and if you have any ideas/suggestions.
> > >
> > > Best,
> > > Ramnath
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > On Thursday, May 2, 2013 11:18:00 PM UTC-4, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> > > > The knitr Shiny app by Yihui was really cool but also a huge security hole--I hope you are only recommending it for local use and only when properly protected by a firewall!
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Wed, May 1, 2013 at 3:58 PM, Ramnath Vaidyanathan <ramnath...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > My question is about how to save shiny rendered html pages. I am not sure this is the right forum to put this question, but I still wanted to try.
> > > > >
> > > > > To give you some context, I just added a Shiny based app to rCharts, adapting the excellent Shiny app put together by @yihui for knitr. It allows users to embed d3js charts in an R Notebook. Here is a screencast for those interested, http://youtu.be/MqMkCk-nc6k,  but if you just want to see it in action, type this from your R console.
> > > > >
> > > > > devtools::install_github('rCharts', 'ramnathv')
> > > > > rCharts::open_notebook()
> > > > >
> > > > > Now, I want to add a feature that allows a user to click on a publish button, that automatically publishes the source Rmd (from the text area) and the shiny rendered HTML to a github repo. I can generate static HTML independent of Shiny using Slidify, but I thought it would simplify the workflow considerably if a user can tweak the source using the notebook, and when happy with the end-product can hit publish.
> > > > >
> > > > > This might be a question for the javascript community, but if any of you have thoughts on how to do this, I would appreciate it.
> > > > >
> > > > > Best,
> > > > > Ramnath

messages.subject: Re: access to shiny server
messages.body_plain:
Is your friend connected to the same local network? The address 192.168.10.103 is an address which will be visible within your local network, but it won't be visible from the rest of the internet. It sounds like you are connected to a wireless router. You can think of the router as joining two networks: the internet, and a local network for your computers. Computers on the internet won't be able to connect to servers on the local network.

If you want to run your own server that is visible on the internet, the best route is to use a hosting service like Amazon EC2.

-Winston

Ramnath

On Sunday, May 5, 2013 9:23:33 AM UTC-4, Ramnath Vaidyanathan wrote:
> I am in the process of building the viewer. While building it, I realized that I can do it purely in Javascript, since there is no necessity for interaction with R, as we are going to be disabling any ability to run arbitrary code. I will put a working prototype on github soon, and can then make the call if there are advantages to hosting it on a Shiny server.
>
> Ramnath
>
>
> On Friday, May 3, 2013 3:38:53 PM UTC-4, Ramnath Vaidyanathan wrote:
> > Let me understand this correctly. When I run any Shiny app on localhost:8100, it can be accessed by others? What steps can I take to ensure that this does not happen? I have been running all kinds of localhost applications, without being aware of this problem.
> >
> > About the viewer, yes, that is what I had in mind. I will get rid of the server.R  code that does the knitting, completely, so that there is no way anyone can knit the Rmd file. All it would do is to load the Rmd file on the left pane and the HTML on the right pane, with links to download the source Rmd and the HTML. A utility function would then allow a user to load the Rmd file into a local shiny instance, and modify it and watch the HTML change.
> >
> > Let me put a rough draft of this together and send you the code, so that you can review it and give me some feedback.
> >
> > Best,
> > Ramnath
> >
> >
> > On Friday, May 3, 2013 12:41:13 PM UTC-6, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> > > With local use and no firewall, anyone who can see your machine could point their browser to http://your-hostname:8100 and get access to the app.
> > >
> > > Your viewer would work, just make sure that you don't merely disable the UI, but also conditionalize the server.R code so that the knitting can never happen. If you only disable the UI, it would still be possible for an attacker to make JavaScript calls that would simulate the clicking of the knit button or whatever. If you end up building this I can review the code for you.
> > >
> > >
> > > On Fri, May 3, 2013 at 12:19 AM, Ramnath Vaidyanathan <ramnath...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Yes. I am only recommending it for local use. Can you elaborate on the firewall issue? How does it affect local use?
> > > >
> > > > I had an idea for using the app only as a viewer, when online. In other words, the online version would load both *.Rmd and *.html in side-by-side windows just like Yihui's app, and will have all the features enabled, except that the knit button will be disabled. So a user can only view the source and the output online, NOT be able to run any code.
> > > >
> > > > In addition, a download button on the top (similar to nbViewer) would allow users to download the Rmd, and a utility function will allow a user to recreate it locally using Shiny. I believe, this would entail the same risks as running runGitHub or runApp or sourcing any external script. I understand that the HTML can have malicious code as well, but I believe that possibility exists on any website that a user visits.
> > > >
> > > > Let me know what you think, and if you have any ideas/suggestions.
> > > >
> > > > Best,
> > > > Ramnath
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Thursday, May 2, 2013 11:18:00 PM UTC-4, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> > > > > The knitr Shiny app by Yihui was really cool but also a huge security hole--I hope you are only recommending it for local use and only when properly protected by a firewall!
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Wed, May 1, 2013 at 3:58 PM, Ramnath Vaidyanathan <ramnath...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > My question is about how to save shiny rendered html pages. I am not sure this is the right forum to put this question, but I still wanted to try.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > To give you some context, I just added a Shiny based app to rCharts, adapting the excellent Shiny app put together by @yihui for knitr. It allows users to embed d3js charts in an R Notebook. Here is a screencast for those interested, http://youtu.be/MqMkCk-nc6k,  but if you just want to see it in action, type this from your R console.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > devtools::install_github('rCharts', 'ramnathv')
> > > > > > rCharts::open_notebook()
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Now, I want to add a feature that allows a user to click on a publish button, that automatically publishes the source Rmd (from the text area) and the shiny rendered HTML to a github repo. I can generate static HTML independent of Shiny using Slidify, but I thought it would simplify the workflow considerably if a user can tweak the source using the notebook, and when happy with the end-product can hit publish.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > This might be a question for the javascript community, but if any of you have thoughts on how to do this, I would appreciate it.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Best,
> > > > > > Ramnath

messages.subject: Re: How to display progressbar in Shiny index.html?
messages.subject_clean: How to display progressbar in Shiny index.html?
messages.body_plain:
There's not a great way to do this right now, the easiest would be to make a custom output binding that looks like textOutputBinding but overrides the showProgress method. Now to actually update the % completion of the progress bar, you need the not-yet-documented session$sendJavascript or session$sendCustomMessage features; there are examples in Winston's testapp repository ; see the message-handler folders and sendjs as well. In the future we hope to be able to provide better progress indicator APIs and widgets right in the framework. messages.subject: Re: Display MathML equations
messages.body_plain:
Yes, you can use MathJax <http://www.mathjax.org/>.

You need to add the following to your ui.R (in the sidebar or mainPanel):

    tags$head(

      tags$script(src = 'https://c328740.ssl.cf1.rackcdn.com/mathjax/2.0-latest/MathJax.js?config=TeX-AMS-MML_HTMLorMML', type = 'text/javascript')

    ),

Then use an htmlOutput in your ui.R, for example:

htmlOutput("equation")

And in your server.R:

output$equation <- reactive({
  generateMathMLString()
})

messages.subject: Re: Extended, multi-application session support?
messages.body_plain:
I don't think reinstalling RStudio will help. What version of R do you have installed on Ubuntu?

I can't say that something as complicated as Rcommander is in the "sweet spot" of what we're trying to accomplish with Shiny. However, I don't know of any limitations in Shiny that would prevent you from doing so. Vincent Nijs has built probably the most complicated Shiny app so far, you can see it here <https://github.com/mostly-harmless/radyant>.

That being said, tcl/tk or even conventional web development techniques plus something like OpenCPU, are probably going to be less risky, though probably more work and more difficult to manage complexity-wise. In other words, I believe Shiny might be easier and more robust until you hit its limitations, which we don't really know yet what they are.

Sorry not to have a more definitive answer for you. Would it be possible to just use Rcommander or Deducer as they exist today, and write a plugin that works with one of them?

messages.subject: Re: returning multiple objects
messages.body_plain:
That's a fine way to do it (see below for caveat), though I'd make it a named list and also pass local=TRUE to source:

main = reactive( {
> blah
> source(filename, local=TRUE)
>
> data_frames = list(raw_data=raw_data, summary_v1=summary_v1, model_output=model_output)

})

Then to refer to those dataframes:

  output$temp = renderTable( {
    t1 = main()$raw_data
    function(t1)
    t1
  })

Now, it only makes sense to source your file inside a reactive if your calculations actually depend on other reactives (input$xxx, for example). If not, you may as well just do the calculation outside of a reactive and directly reference those calculated variables in the render functions. Render functions can read non-reactive values just fine; they (the non-reactive values) just won't trigger the render function to re-execute, that's all.

messages.subject: Re: Actionbutton
messages.body_plain:
This should work, unless the "published" textOutput is not visible (or it is visible and for some reason Shiny mistakenly thinks it is not visible--we had bugs in this area before, but don't believe we have any bugs in the current master branch on GitHub). But even if it works, I wouldn't say this is the "Shiny way" to do it--renderText blocks should generally be side-effect-free, i.e. the calculation is only interesting in what it returns.

If you are interested in the side effects of the renderText body (which in this case we are--knitting and publishing are side effects, e.g. they aren't reflected in the return value) then in general you do NOT want to put that code in an output. Instead, create an observer:
observe({

  if (input$publish != 0){

    isolate({
      gist <- createGist(list(

        'index.Rmd' = input$nbSrc,

        'index.html' = createHTML(input$nbSrc)

      ))

      postGist(gist)

    })

  }
})

The return values of observe blocks are always discarded, so you can't directly use this to indicate whether the operation succeeded or not (for example). However, you can use observer code to set reactive values (basically a hashtable with reactive properties, that you create using reactiveValues()) that are then used to update text outputs.

For much more about observers and reactive values, please see http://rstudio.github.io/shiny/tutorial/#reactivity-overview

messages.subject: Re: sending RGL output to Shiny (non-interactively)
messages.body_plain:
Oh, hm, I didn't realize that rgl needs to have a running X device to even load the package.

Using the instructions in Jeff's blog post is probably not a good idea for multi-user systems like glimmer (and our new server, spark) -- it's probably a security hole to have a single X session for the shiny-server process that is used by all apps.

It's possible for each user to start a Xvfb (X virtual frame buffer) device, but this could lead to other problems. There's no guarantee that Xvfb will be closed properly when an app is closed, and this could lead to many, many running X sessions on glimmer, especially since there are so many users.

I'll look into this a bit more to see if there's a better way to use rgl on multi-user system like glimmer and spark.

-Winston

messages.subject: Repositioning The Side Scroll Bar
messages.body_plain:
Hey all,

I have a recurring issue where on occasion there will be so many samples in a plot that it stretches the page horizontally, which itself isn't much of a concern.  The problem is that the horizontal scroll bar is only visible when scrolling to the bottom of the page.  So at a glance, it may not be obvious that some of the plots are actually going off the page horizontally.

So the solution I would like to achieve is having the sideways scroll bar always visible if/when the page needs one.

Thanks!
Mike

It looks like the server is fine, but the app isn't doing so well, because Shiny Server currently starts a single R process for each app, which is shared across all client sessions. messages.subject: Re: The path collected by fileInput
messages.body_plain:
The problem is file.choose() only launches a dialog when running in an interactive session of R, which is not the case when R is running under Shiny Server. You can see this yourself if you run R non-interactively from your command line:

R -e "file.choose()"

I'm not sure how you can work around this--maybe someone else has ideas?

messages.subject: twitteR and shiny - sending tweets with shiny
messages.subject_clean: twitteR and shiny - sending tweets with shiny
messages.body_plain:
Hi. I've been developing a system where I use twitter as a sort of temporal data store... basically, I define a syntax for data I want to log and use twitter to log it on the go with my phone (why? ... using twitter like this, I don't have to build an interface and database just to save data on the go - it's all there on twitter waiting for me to download it, timestamped and all).

The, I download the most recent tweets and munge the data from there, which then gets published in a shiny app in the form of graphs and information and all that fun business.

I use the 'twitteR' and 'ROAuth' packages to access twitter. It would be great if I could send tweets from the shiny interface as well. I haven't found a way to send a tweet from R yet. I've seen and tried some old stackoverflow code <http://stackoverflow.com/questions/4252694/using-r-to-send-tweets>, but it did not seem to work.

Like I said, not so much a shiny question, but any help would do - and I've seen some people talking about twitteR and ROAuth (and streamR, which I hadn't heard of) lately.

Thanks for reading,

Dan

Dear Ramnath and Joe:

I'm not sure whether I should start a new thread or just reply here... for the sake of simplicity, I reply here, since it's somewhat related.

First of all: I'm a newbie using Shiny, and it was yesterday when I installed shiny locally for the first time, and today when I run my first example, etc. (even if I've been reading about Shiny since 6 months ago, at least! :-))

One of my first goals while learning Shiny was to call and display a simple shiny app on a server, in a similar way to what I managed to do with your package rNVD3 ( http://ramnathv.github.io/rNVD3/ ).

In that case with rNVD3, I followed your "Example 2: Stacked bar Plot", but saving the html to disk (with p1$save('foo.html') instead of p1$printChart('foo.html') ). And then, loading it in a wiki page  with an iframe to display that html saved on disk. A working proof-of-concept reusing your rNVD3 package:
http://r-es.org/r_test8

The Web platform to manage the whole thing is called Tiki ( https://tiki.org ), and the communication with R is handled by PluginR ( https://doc.tiki.org/PluginR )

Then, I wanted to do achieve something similar with a Shiny app. And since you have also an equivalent example in your page http://ramnathv.github.io/rNVD3/ ("Using it with Shiny"), then I wanted to follow with your example.

But, I haven't found a function in shiny to save to disk the whole html page of the app produced.

Is this planned in the development roadmap of Shiny?
Am I trying to follow a wrong path or missing something important here? (that might also be the case, since I'm fairly newbie with all this!)

Any hints on my goal to display shiny apps from (wiki) html pages controlled by something else than shiny server (Tiki, in this case)?

Xavier

P.S: By the way, nice video showing your proof-of-concept, Ramnath! I'm very impressed also with your work! (as well as the work with Shiny, of course!)

messages.subject: Re: Saving Shiny Rendered HTML
messages.body_plain:
First off, nice work embedding it in a Wiki. A key objective of rCharts is to make it easy to share charts and this is a great way to do it.

Coming to Shiny apps, they need to be run off a Shiny server. So, one way to embed a shiny app is to put it in an iframe. For example, you can include this app http://glimmer.rstudio.com/ramnathv/strikeouts/ by inserting it into an iframe tag. Shiny apps cannot be saved as standalone HTMLs.

If you are running a Shiny server on Tiki, then it should be possible to copy the code in the app directory and directly render the app on Tiki.

Hope this is useful.

Cheers,
Ramnath

Well, yes, I'm running (I think) shiny-server in the same server where Tiki is (or I can get it installed). My question is how to easily "save" the html (or the ui.R and server.R) from the r script itself, so that I can have users in wiki platforms collaboratively create and edit their shiny apps.

About security (obvious concern inthis context, of course), PluginR checks for "potentially dangerous" (server-wise) commands, and in case any of those are found in the r script in the wiki page, the r script (plugin R call) needs to be validated by an admin of the Tiki installation. And admins permissions in the Tiki should be shared only with people that you would share you ssh login credentials to your server.

So, any equivalent p1$save for a shiny app, that can save the ui.R and server.R server-side wherever you tell them to be stored (after admin validation)?

Is it clearer now my question?

Xavier

messages.subject: Re: Saving Shiny Rendered HTML
messages.body_plain:
Creating, editing, and saving ui.R and server.R files does not involve Shiny itself--these are merely inputs to the Shiny app. You could handle all of that in PHP.

Does PluginR allow the use of arbitrary packages? (From a security perspective I hope the answer is no!)

Speaking of security, another reason this might not be a great idea is because users can then easily write JavaScript snippets that can be served up on your domain, which would allow them to steal logon credentials (see XSS <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-site_scripting>). In order to avoid this you would need to ensure that your Shiny apps are served from a different domain than the rest of the wiki.

messages.subject: Re: Repositioning The Side Scroll Bar
messages.body_plain:
Looks like Bootstrap's tab panel doesn't want you to let content inside expand the size of the tab panel--that's a reasonable decision on their part I think.

Try adding this somewhere in your sidebarPanel or mainPanel (doesn't matter where):

tags$style(type="text/css", ".tab-content { overflow: visible; }")

If that doesn't work then try this instead:

tags$style(type="text/css", ".tab-content { overflow: visible !important; }")

messages.subject: Re: Force size of 'device window'
messages.body_plain:
Wow, it actually is possible now.

In ui.R:

plotOutput("foo", height="auto")

In server.R:

output$foo({
  # create plot
}, height=function() { session$clientdata$output_foo_width * 1.0 })

You can modify "1.0" in the last line to get a different aspect ratio. And make sure to change "output_foo_width" to replace "foo" with your plot's ID.

You also have to modify the line
    shinyServer(function(input, output) {
to be
    shinyServer(function(input, output, session) {

If you get errors from the above then you may need to upgrade to a more recent build of Shiny than is on CRAN; try installing it from GitHub:

install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("shiny", "rstudio")

By default, outputs (including renderUI/uiOutput) are suspended when they're not visible -- you may find it useful to disable this behavior in your case. In your server code you could have something like this:

output$ui_out <- renderUI({ ... })

  headerPanel("Integrated search interface for gene queries"),

  sidebarPanel(
    textInput("SNP", "rs ID of SNP of interest"),

    helpText("separate genotype with a space (e.g. A A)"),

    textInput("number", "Number of samples needed (in descending order of stock)"),

    submitButton("Submit")
    ), #end sidebar
  mainPanel(

     tableOutput("outputResults")

    )
  )#end pageWithSideBar
        ) #end shinyUI

--
server.R
--

require(shiny)
require(RMySQL)

driver <- dbDriver("MySQL")
connection <- dbConnect(MySQL(), user="fgl", host="localhost", password="fgl",dbname="fgl")
#genotype <- read.csv(genotype.csv) #read in genotype excel spreadsheet as csv for export to mySQL
#dbWriteTable(connection, "genotypes", genotype)

options(shiny.maxRequestSize=-1)
shinyServer(function(input,output){
  statement<- reactive({

              x <- as.character(input$SNP)
              y <- as.character(input$haplotype)

              sprintf("SELECT IID, %s FROM genotypes WHERE %s = '%s'",x,x,y)
           })

             resultSamples <-reactive(dbGetQuery(connection, statement()))

             checkSurvey <-dbGetQuery(connection,"SELECT Sample_ID,  Stock_DNA__ul_ ,Amp_DNA_conc__ng_ul_  , Amp_DNA__ul_  FROM survey")
             resultStocks <- reactive({
               z <- as.character(input$number)
               a <- checkSurvey[checkSurvey$Sample_ID %in% resultSamples()$IID,]
               b <- a[order(-a$Stock_DNA__ul_),]
               c <- b[1:z,]
             })

             output$outputResults <- renderTable(resultStocks())

              }

            )
--

Thanks again for your time!

Jeremy

I understand that this is not exactly what shiny has been built for (what I actually need is a desktop GUI, so probably tcltk would be more appropriate for this task), but I made some tests and shiny behaves quite well for my purposes, and the pages are very easy to code.

So I have three questions:

1 - do you think using shiny for developing desktop-like GUIs is could to lead to problems/limitations?

2 - is there a quick way to make the pages accessible only to the user that spawned them?

3 - is there a way to make runApp select the first available port instead of the default?

Thanks a lot.

messages.subject: Re: Saving Shiny Rendered HTML
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joe:

On 10/05/13 19:11, Joe Cheng wrote:
> Creating, editing, and saving ui.R and server.R files does not involve Shiny itself--these are merely inputs to the Shiny app. You could handle all of that in PHP.
>

Ok, thanks for the clarifications. I slowly understanding better how to use Shiny.

> Does PluginR allow the use of arbitrary packages? (From a security perspective I hope the answer is no!)
>

Well, in fact, the answer is yes. There is a list of commands which  are stopped until an admin validates the call, but all the other R commands are allowed to the users of the Tiki installation.
This way to aim to combine some more level of security in collaborative platforms in which you can run R scripts (similarly to what was implemented in the mediawiki r extension, etc).

Potentially dangerous commands catched by PluginR:
http://sourceforge.net/p/tikiwiki/code/HEAD/tree/mods/trunk/wiki-plugins/r/lib/wiki-plugins/wikiplugin_rr.php

lines 662 - 702

If you know of any other commands potentially dangerous (Server-wise), I'll be glad to add them to the ones that require admin validation.

> Speaking of security, another reason this might not be a great idea is because users can then easily write JavaScript snippets that can be served up on your domain, which would allow them to steal logon credentials (see XSS <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-site_scripting>). In order to avoid this you would need to ensure that your Shiny apps are served from a different domain than the rest of the wiki.
>

Aha, good point. However, with the security model in Tiki, any javascript snippet would need to be validated by an admin, so that, as far as I understand, this is not a special security concern within Tiki.

If any benevolent hacker can make a proof of concept of exploit of Tiki & PluginR, you can try the community site for R users in Spain:
https://r-es.org

It's in Spanish, though. However, once registered and logged in, anyone can switch the language of the interface for his/her user to English, for instance.

Our basic idea, is that Shiny is excellent to produce standalone web interfaces for R apps, with wonderful "reactivity". While Tiki is best suited to deploy full Wiki/CMS/Groupware sites for documentation, blogging, discussing, with support for R syntax highlighting, etc. and while still allowing to create web 2.0 interfaces for R scripts (even if without the reactive model of Shiny).

So I will still explore someway to get shiny reactive interfaces through wiki pages in Tiki.

Thanks for your feedback.

Xavier

>
> On Fri, May 10, 2013 at 9:14 AM, Xavier de Pedro <xavier....@vhir.org> wrote:
> > Thanks for your kind words.
> >
> > Well, yes, I'm running (I think) shiny-server in the same server where Tiki is (or I can get it installed). My question is how to easily "save" the html (or the ui.R and server.R) from the r script itself, so that I can have users in wiki platforms collaboratively create and edit their shiny apps.
> >
> > About security (obvious concern inthis context, of course), PluginR checks for "potentially dangerous" (server-wise) commands, and in case any of those are found in the r script in the wiki page, the r script (plugin R call) needs to be validated by an admin of the Tiki installation. And admins permissions in the Tiki should be shared only with people that you would share you ssh login credentials to your server.
> >
> > So, any equivalent p1$save for a shiny app, that can save the ui.R and server.R server-side wherever you tell them to be stored (after admin validation)?
> >
> > Is it clearer now my question?
> >
> > Xavier
> >
> >
> >

> > >

> > >

> > > Cheers,
> > > Ramnath
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > On Friday, May 10, 2013 10:55:46 AM UTC-4, Xavier de Pedro wrote:
> > > > Dear Ramnath and Joe:
> > > >
> > > > I'm not sure whether I should start a new thread or just reply here... for the sake of simplicity, I reply here, since it's somewhat related.
> > > >
> > > > First of all: I'm a newbie using Shiny, and it was yesterday when I installed shiny locally for the first time, and today when I run my first example, etc. (even if I've been reading about Shiny since 6 months ago, at least! :-))
> > > >

messages.subject: Re: system() does not seem to work within a shiny app... why is this?
messages.subject_clean: system() does not seem to work within a shiny app... why is this?
messages.body_plain:
It's because reactive expressions are lazily evaluated; since systemCall is never used by anyone, its code is never executed.

You can create an observer to get the code to execute:

observe({ systemCall() })

Or just replace systemCall altogether with:

observe({

  input$txt
  system('ls > tmpFile.txt')
})

You can read more about reactive expressions (aka conductors) and observers (aka endpoints) in the "Reactivity Overview" chapter of the tutorial:
http://rstudio.github.io/shiny/tutorial/#reactivity-overview

Oscar.

messages.subject: Re: Digg.com
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the reminder - here are the main changes we made to improve performance:

The primary bottleneck for Andrew's app was that, each time someone wanted to view data for a show, it fetched the data from a remote website, which was not particularly fast. This was fine for just a few simultaneous users, but not for digg-scale traffic. There were two things we did to help speed it up:

 - Installed the memoise package and, and use it to cache the download results for each show/URL. The memoized function was defined _outside_ of the shinyServer() call, so that the cache is shared across all user sessions (see the Scoping section of the tutorial for more info). For more about using memoise, see https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups=#!searchin/shiny-discuss/memoise/shiny-discuss/GPdLbZEN45s/rBcRv9uztYsJ.

 - Although memoization speeds things up, the cache persists only within a R session, so it is lost whenever the app quits or crashes. Unfortunately, crashes happened frequently, due to (A) a bug in shiny server (which is now fixed) and (B) a problem in making plots with extended characters (worked around). Instead of downloading data for each show whenever the app restarted, we wrote a script to download all the data and save it in a subdirectory of the app. After this, the app simply loaded data from local files, so even after a crash, it was fast.

Andrew's app also exposed a bug in selectInput when the same name is shared with more than one choice (fixed):
  https://github.com/rstudio/shiny/issues/157

In general, as the traffic to an app increases, you'll want to cache results and shift more of the work to be done ahead of time, before the user visits. The kinds of things you'll want to handle this way include expensive computations and slow network transfers. If traffic is very high, it might also help to pre-render images, save them, and send them with renderImage(), instead of using renderPlot().

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: sending RGL output to Shiny (non-interactively)
messages.body_plain:
Sorry, identify() won't work, since it needs to talk directly to the graphic device, but Shiny apps show the plots through the browser. I know this doesn't help now, but the future of interactive graphics with Shiny for the graphics to be rendered in the browser, which will make it possible to do things like that.

-Winston

However, when I call that same function from within Shiny, it takes about a thousand times longer to complete, and while it is running, the activity monitor shows that one of my cores is running at 100% with Rstudio is the big user.

Any suggestions as to the cause of this behavior?

messages.subject: Shiny Server as non-root
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This is my first time posting to the Shiny google group, so first of all, thank you so much for developing Shiny. It has really enhanced my workflow, not to mention made it much easier to convince non-statisticians that statistics is cool and fun!

Our organization is hoping to use the Shiny server to host our own Shiny apps. We want to run shiny-server as a non-root user. It looks like this functionality has been implemented in this github branch:

https://github.com/jcheng5/shiny-server/tree/no-su

But we are eager for this functionality to be included in an official release. I thought it would be worth mentioning that this is an important and much desired capability for a really great piece of software. As the stats person who has been making apps with Shiny since January, all seems well and good. But not being a web/IT person, I am pretty much just quoting the needs/wants of others where I work who are more involved in secure web deployment. So unfortunately, I can't comment much on why this is so important, but this is just to let you guys know that it does seem to be our one and only obstacle to using Shiny publicly rather than just on a local development server. Is there any cause for concern or inconveniences over using the github branch above? In terms of eventually having to switch at some point later on from that branch to a later release of shiny-server?

Thanks so much,
Matt

messages.subject_clean: system() does not seem to work within a shiny app... why is this?
messages.body_plain:
thank you Joe

On Tuesday, May 14, 2013 1:47:56 AM UTC-6, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> It's because reactive expressions are lazily evaluated; since systemCall is never used by anyone, its code is never executed.
>
> You can create an observer to get the code to execute:
>
> observe({ systemCall() })
>
> Or just replace systemCall altogether with:
>
> observe({
>   input$txt
>   system('ls > tmpFile.txt')
> })
>
> You can read more about reactive expressions (aka conductors) and observers (aka endpoints) in the "Reactivity Overview" chapter of the tutorial:
> http://rstudio.github.io/shiny/tutorial/#reactivity-overview
>
>
> On Mon, May 13, 2013 at 11:48 AM, Daniel Bowen <count...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > ui.R
> >
> > shinyUI(bootstrapPage(
> >
> >   submitButton(),
> >
> >   textInput('txt', 'text')
> >
> > ))
> >
> >
> > server.R
> >
> > shinyServer(function(input, output) {
> >
> >   systemCall <- reactive({
> >
> >     input$txt
> >
> >     system('ls > tmpFile.txt')
> >
> >   })
> >
> > })
> >
> >
> > ... this is a simplified version of my problem. my full code, has the system() call inside a function that is called by a reactive function in shinyServer.
> >
> > Why does this not work?
> >
> > Thanks, in advanced
> >

messages.subject: Re: shiny-server startup errors
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joe,

I've done some hunting around and asking in the Gentoo community.

On Friday, May 10, 2013 6:28:57 PM UTC+1, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:

>
> shiny-server doesn't create a pid file, it also doesn't daemonize itself by forking though. Is that a problem for gentoo? If so do you have a link that explains how gentoo wants/expects these kind of processes to behave?

The pid file isn't a problem, its possible to have the init script create one on starting the process using a combination of the '--make-pidfile --pidfile "${PIDFILE}"' flags to the start-stop-daemon command.  Its also possible to daemonize the process using the '--background' flag of start-stop-daemon too.  So the init-script is now looking like...

#!/sbin/runscript

PIDFILE=/var/run/shiny-server.pid

depend(){

   after net
}
start(){
   ebegin "Starting shiny-server"

   start-stop-daemon --start --make-pidfile --pidfile "${PIDFILE}" \
    --background --exec /usr/bin/shiny-server >> /var/log/shiny-server.log 2>&1

    local _retval=$?
    eend "${_retval}"
}
stop(){
   ebegin "Stopping shiny-server"

   start-stop-daemon --stop --pidfile "${PIDFILE}"

   local _retval=$?
   eend "${_retval}"
}

...and it appears to work fine with the examples.

Hope thats useful, I'll update/feedback when I make some progress on writing an ebuild to install shiny-server on Gentoo (a new learning curve for me though).

Neil

messages.subject: conditionalPanel based on fileInput
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am trying to build a page where the user uploads a file and then a model is fit based on that input file. I want some of the UI to depend on the content of the file. So far I have:

ui.R

    fileInput("dataFile", "Data file", multiple=FALSE, accept="text/csv"),
    uiOutput("speciesList")

server.R

  get.data <- reactive({
    if (is.null(input$dataFile)) {
      # if no data file is uploaded, return NULL
      d <- NULL
    } else {
      # otherwise read the data and return the data.frame
      dataFile <- input$dataFile$datapath
      d <- read.data(dataFile, filetype="csv")
    }
    d
  })

  # Get list of species
  output$speciesList <- renderUI({
    d <- get.data()
    sp <- names(d)[-c(1,2)]
    if (!is.null(sp)) selectInput("species", "Species to model", sp)
  })

I would like to get the dependency logic (the fact that the list of species cannot be generate if a file has not been uploaded yet) outside of the server code (all those if conditions) and inside the UI, because I think this is where the belongs (the server should know how to read the file, the UI should tell it when to do so).

So I tried wrapping uiOutput("speciesList") in a conditionalPanel that way:

    conditionalPanel(
      condition="typeof(input.dataFile) != 'undefined'",
      uiOutput("speciesList")
    ),

where typeof != undefined is supposed to test wether input.dataFile is null. Indeed, it is null before anything is uploaded. My problems are:
- I am not sure that javascript condition is valid
- when I inspect the page of my shiny app with the JavaScript console (in Chrome if that matters) the dataFile input value (window.Shiny.shinyapp.$inputValues.dataFile) stays null even after I upload a file.

How should one's UI depend on a file being uploaded?

Thanks in advance,

Jean-Olivier Irisson

messages.subject: Re: best practices for modular Shiny app development?
messages.subject_clean: best practices for modular Shiny app development?
messages.body_plain:
The main thing for me (sofar) was to try to keep ui.R manageable.

In ui.R I have a line:

uiOutput("ui_analysis")

That calls a function defined in server.R (see below). I put all analysis tools I want to use into a directory (tools/ in this case). These are sourced when the app is started up. I then have a tools.html file that, basically, determines which ui elements get shown. Ideally I would want tools.html to be created automatically based on what is in the tools/ directory. Haven't gotten that far yet but suggestions on how to do this cleanly are welcome.

Code is here:

https://github.com/mostly-harmless/radyant

I hope Alex will pitch in as well. His approach is likely to be a bit more sophisticated than mine.

Keep us posted as you make progress with your app.

shinyServer(function(input, output) {

# source base functions
source('radyant.R', local = TRUE)

# source enabled analysis tools
flist <- sourceDirectory('tools', recursive = TRUE)

# the 'grand' analysis ui-element caller
output$ui_analysis <- renderUI({
   if(input$tool == "dataview") return()
 get(paste('ui_',input$tool, sep=""))()
})
})

> > >
> > > My next largest concern, which I have not yet come to an elegant solution for, is a matter of reproducible research.  It all boils down to being able to track the user and be able to follow their steps to produce the same results.  The issues that have come up are 1) The code used for shiny would have to be manually altered to get rid of shiny specific functions and mechanics in order to run through as an R script (I presume?),  2) The user is likely to want to save multiple plots generated with each plot function with the shiny program, so simply using the last available reactives and inputs$s will not suffice,  3) The user inputs are not likely to be linearly performed (user goes through steps 1-7, decides to change something in step 4 and continues from that point forward again) and 4) the R history saved appears to just be the runApp() function, at least when run locally.
> > >
> > > The practical reasons for needing reproducibility could be as simple as a collaborator comes to me and says "I made this plot yesterday with the application you made, I think I used the following criteria, could you please make it again with the following custom changes to it?" or "I made this plot a couple months ago, and I performed some independent validation and would like to publish it- could you provide the code used to produce it for the supplemental portion?"

I should start by stating that I haven't built any Shiny apps of the magnitude that Vincent or Alex have built. However, I thought that it would be useful to share my approach, since it is a bit different from their approaches.

My app is usually structured in the following fashion

|- apps
|- www
|------libraries
|----- index.Rmd
|----- index.html
|- server.R

All apps are single files in the app folder, which are sourced into server.R, which is generic

require(shiny)
shinyServer(function(input, output){
  addResourcePath('libraries', 'www/libraries')
  apps = dir("apps", pattern = '^app', full = T)
  for (app in apps){
    source(app, local = TRUE)
  }
})

I prefer to use the HTML UI, especially when I have a lot of text. I use Slidify to convert index.Rmd to index.html in the www folder.

You will find an example of this approach in this github repo https://github.com/ramnathv/shinySlidify, which you can run using

runUrl("https://github.com/ramnathv/shinySlidify/archive/gh-pages.zip")

Note that the page layout can be changed easily as Slidify supports multiple frameworks. So you can do a bootstrap page instead of slide deck.

Best,
Ramnath

On Thursday, May 16, 2013 6:46:26 PM UTC+1, Sam wrote:

<snip>

> curl http://nodejs.org/dist/node-latest.tar.gz | tar xz --strip-components=1
>
> Got this issue when executed the above command - > curl: (6) Couldn't resolve host 'nodejs.org <http://nodejs.org>'

This is a network or DNS resolution problem - are you sure your system is connected to the network with Internet access? If it is, then try typing this command:

host nodejs.org <http://nodejs.org>

and you should see something like this:

nodejs.org <http://nodejs.org> has address 165.225.133.150
nodejs.org <http://nodejs.org> mail is handled by 10 mail.nodejs.org <http://mail.nodejs.org>.

If this does not work or you receive an error message, maybe your /etc/resolv.conf file is missing or incorrectly configured. If it's missing, just create one containing the line:

nameserver 8.8.8.8

and this should work. If the file is present, try changing it to read 'nameserver 8.8.8.8' as described above. If having done this you still can't resolve the IP address for nodejs.org <http://nodejs.org> then perhaps your /etc/nsswitch.conf is incorrect but this is not very common.

Hope this helps with this part of the installation...

Regarding seeing/adjusting the HTML, the easiest way is to just View Source in your web browser.

Another way is to take any subexpression in ui.R, and call cat(as.character(...)) on it. For example,
  cat(as.character(textInput("foo", "Foo")))
prints out
  <label for="foo">Foo</label>
  <input id="foo" type="text" value=""/>

The functions called in shinyUI are just list-generating code; they return data structures that represent HTML and can be manipulated. See the ?tagList, ?tags, and ?HTML help topics. Here's one example:

messages.body_plain:
After the input changes, the next time histoGraph() is called, the histoGraph code is actually executed. After that, but before the next input change, each call to histoGraph() just returns the previous value (i.e. the value is cached until invalidation).

The problem is that the plot will only show up in the browser if histoGraph actually executes while inside renderPlot. If renderTable happens to run first, then histoGraph is going to execute outside of a renderPlot. This matters because renderPlot sets up a png() R graphics device when it starts executing its code block, and closes it when it's done.

I can't tell from looking at your code, though, what line is actually causing the histogram to be drawn; is it rxHistogram? It does a plot but also returns some data? You would need to separate those out into two separate pieces of functionality, where the latter is in the reactive({}) and the former is directly in renderPlot.

Another minor note, the calls to outputOptions only need to execute once each, so they should be moved to after the definition of their respective outputs, not nested inside of the definition.

messages.subject: Re: function visibility in shiny pages
messages.body_plain:
You can call unexported functions with package:::function(). Note that there are three colons - if there were two colons, it could only call exported functions. It's generally frowned upon to call unexported functions from a package (because the unexported, internal functions in a package might change over time), but I guess if you are only doing it within your own package, that's not so bad.

Another possibility is, instead of putting your functions in a package the normal way (in the R/ directory), you can put them in the inst/ directory of your package, and then source them in each app, with something like this:
  source(system.file("sharedfunctions.r", package="mypackage"), local=TRUE)

-Winston

  values$histObj <- histObj

outputOptions(output, "histoPlot", suspendWhenHidden=FALSE)

messages.body_plain:
That's an extremely general question, as it depends almost entirely on what you're doing with the data. If you're rendering a plot from it, then quite a lot of data, since all that is being sent to the browser is the rendered plot image.

messages.subject: Re: Is it possible to use web images directly with renderImage()?
messages.subject_clean: Is it possible to use web images directly with renderImage()?
messages.body_plain: Just want to point out that this is a very bad habit to get into: output$image = renderPrint({ src = input$image_url cat(sprintf('', src)) }) This is far safer: output$image = renderUI({ src = input$image_url tags$img(src=src) }) The problem with the first snippet is that in the future we will add 1) authentication, and 2) the ability to control inputs via URL parameters. So someone could get you to click on a link like this: http://yourserver/yourapp/?input.image_url=> which would allow whoever owns the evil server to log in to the Shiny Server instance as you (at least temporarily). This is a textbook cross site scripting vulnerability, which is caused by user-generated content being inserted indiscriminately into secure web pages. The second snippet doesn't have this problem, because when you use Shiny's HTML building functions like tags$img, attribute values are properly escaped. So the img tag won't succeed in loading an image, but it also won't allow JavaScript to be inserted into the page no matter what the attacker puts into input$image_url. We'll try to have this stuff written up, as I'm sure many/most Shiny users have not had to worry much about secure web coding practices before. On Friday, May 17, 2013 7:35:46 PM UTC-4, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote: > Just want to point out that this is a very bad habit to get into: > > > > output$image = renderPrint({ > src = input$image_url > > > cat(sprintf('', src)) > > > }) > > This is far safer: > > output$image = renderUI({ > > > src = input$image_url > tags$img(src=src) > > > }) > > The problem with the first snippet is that in the future we will add 1) authentication, and 2) the ability to control inputs via URL parameters. So someone could get you to click on a link like this: > > http://yourserver/yourapp/?input.image_url=> > > which would allow whoever owns the evil server to log in to the Shiny Server instance as you (at least temporarily). messages.subject_clean: Multiple users on same app with long running processes
messages.body_plain:
The current version of shiny-server is limited to this model, where all users of a given app share the same process. The commercial version of shiny-server (beta coming this summer) will have additional deployment options, such as one-process-per-user; that should be what you want.

messages.subject: plotmath expressions - different behavior on server vs. local host
messages.subject_clean: plotmath expressions - different behavior on server vs. local host
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have an example Shiny app here that I am working on:
http://shiny.snap.uaf.edu/RV_distributionsV4/

I have added probability density and mass functions to my plots using plotmath expressions. What I have found is that when I run the app on my pc using local host, the expressions plot nicely. However, once that app is run using shiny-server, the notation is not so nice, particularly with commas and minus signs and such overlapping with other text and symbols and being in the wrong place in the displayed equations. For example, if you click on the normal distribution at the link above and look at the displayed pdf and support, you can see the issue.

Normally I would just dig into my code and see what is wrong, and perhaps there is a better way I can make an expression, but I feel like on a fundamental level, there should be nothing necessarily wrong with the R code, as the same code from the version of the same copy of the app I have on github, displays properly using local host but a bit messy using shiny-server. Please let me know if code would be helpful or anything else I can provide. Does anyone know of why this different plotmath behavior may be occurring? I've attached a screenshot of how the plot annotation displays when I run the same app using a local host.

Thanks,
Matt

I just tried using that expression in generating a PNG, using png() and CairoPNG() from the Cairo package, on Linux.

By default, if you have the Cairo package installed, it will use CairoPNG() instead of png(), because the former has better support for antialiasing, so the output generally looks better. Unfortunately, the math expressions look worse with CairoPNG() -- on Linux, at least.

I'd recommend uninstalling the Cairo package and seeing if that helps.

Here's the code I used, and I've attached the output files.

library(Cairo)

cexpr.norm <- expression(
  italic(
    paste(
displaystyle(f(x)~"="~frac(1,sqrt(2*pi*sigma^scriptscriptstyle("2")))~e^{frac(-1,2*sigma^{scriptscriptstyle("2")})*(x-mu)^scriptscriptstyle("2")})
      ~~~~displaystyle(list(paste(-infinity<x) <infinity, atop(paste(-infinity<mu) <infinity, paste(0<sigma^scriptscriptstyle("2")) <infinity)))
    )
  )
)

png('math_png.png')
matplot(1:4,1:4, main = cexpr.norm)
dev.off()

CairoPNG('math_CairoPNG.png')
matplot(1:4,1:4, main = cexpr.norm)
dev.off()

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: problem: place an input$variable in SQL query
messages.subject_clean: problem: place an input$variable in SQL query
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stratos, it looks like your renderTable code block is evaluating to a character vector, not a data frame. If you provide more code we may be able to help.

You also need to be very, very careful when integrating user input into your SQL queries. If your code looks like this:

sqlQuery(paste0("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = '", input$variable, "';"), ... )

then the user could type in something like

'; DELETE FROM users;

which would result in the sqlQuery call executing two SQL statements, the latter of which would erase all data from the users table. This is called a SQL injection attack <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SQL_injection> and is one of the most commonly exploited security flaws in web applications.

The quick fix is to make sure that input$variable is SQL escaped <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SQL_injection#Escaping>. I'm not sure if RODBC provides an escaping function.

The better fix is to use parameterized queries, so the above would become:

sqlQuery("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?;", input$variable, ...)

but I don't think RODBC works that way (someone please correct me if I'm wrong).

Can anyone with some RODBC experience weigh in about the right way to do this?

messages.subject: Re: Change Color of sliderInput's slider bar?
messages.subject_clean: Change Color of sliderInput's slider bar?
messages.body_plain:
You can create a subdirectory "www" under your application directory, and place a .css file there. Then reference it from your ui.R. For example,

~/myapp/ui.R
~/myapp/server.R
~/myapp/www/styles.css

In your ui.R you can put a tags$link anywhere, for example in mainPanel:

mainPanel(
  tags$link(rel="stylesheet", type="text/css", href="styles.css"),
  # more controls go here...
)

That tags$link will become:
<link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="styles.css"/>

Notice that while your styles.css is stored in a www directory, you do not reference "www" in your link tag.

You are right. Here is a modified version that should work. It behaves  just like includeMarkdown, and does not write any intermediate files. You can insert mathjax directly inside includeRmd, by doing html <- paste(html, mathjax_script, collapse = '\n').

includeRmd <- function(path){
  if (!require(knitr))
    stop("knitr package is not installed")
  if (!require(markdown))
    stop("Markdown package is not installed")
  shiny:::dependsOnFile(path)

  contents = paste(readLines(path, warn = FALSE), collapse = '\n')
  html <- knitr::knit2html(text = contents, fragment.only = TRUE)
  Encoding(html) <- 'UTF-8'
  return(HTML(html))
}

messages.subject: Re: New isolate feature (helps with actionButton)
messages.body_plain:
Can it help with my problem mentioned here and how?

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/16670908/r-shiny-multiple-tabpanel-in-tabsetpanel-not-loading

On Saturday, January 5, 2013 12:28:20 AM UTC+3, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> A number of you have tried to use the actionButton that's included in shiny-incubator to perform actions, and sometimes those actions needed to read from other reactive inputs. Until now, changes to those other inputs would cause the action to be re-executed, with no clean way to suppress those extra executions.
>
> We just checked in a change to the GitHub repository that should improve things quite a bit. I'm not sure this will be our final solution to this problem, but welcome your feedback.
>
> The change is a new function called "isolate", and it lets you execute code that reads from reactive values/functions, without having their reactivity "infect" the caller.
>
> So a reactive data frame that only recalculates itself when an action button (with the id "recalcButton") is pressed might look like this:
>
> mydata <- reactive(function() {
>   # Don't do anything until after the first button push.
>   if (input$recalcButton == 0)
>     return(NULL)
>
>   # Note that just by virtue of checking the value of input$recalcButton,
>   # we're now going to get called whenever it is pushed.
>
>   return(isolate({
>     # Now do the expensive stuff
>     foo <- activateInterlock(input$foo)
>     bar <- connectDynotherm(input$bar)
>     baz <- bringInfracellsUp(input$baz)
>     c(foo=foo, bar=bar, baz=baz)
>   }))
> })
>
> So mydata will automatically react to changes in recalcButton (i.e. when it is pushed) but not to changes in the inputs foo, bar, or baz.
>
> How to install
>
> If you'd like to try isolate out for yourself, you can conveniently install the latest build from github using these commands:
>
> install.package("devtools")  # if necessary
> devtools::install_github("shiny", "rstudio")
>
> (Glimmer users: We generally keep Glimmer synced to the version of Shiny that's on CRAN, so isolate probably won't be available there for at least a couple of weeks. Sorry.)

> On Saturday, January 5, 2013 12:28:20 AM UTC+3, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> > A number of you have tried to use the actionButton that's included in shiny-incubator to perform actions, and sometimes those actions needed to read from other reactive inputs. Until now, changes to those other inputs would cause the action to be re-executed, with no clean way to suppress those extra executions.
> >
> > We just checked in a change to the GitHub repository that should improve things quite a bit. I'm not sure this will be our final solution to this problem, but welcome your feedback.
> >
> > The change is a new function called "isolate", and it lets you execute code that reads from reactive values/functions, without having their reactivity "infect" the caller.
> >
> > So a reactive data frame that only recalculates itself when an action button (with the id "recalcButton") is pressed might look like this:
> >
> > mydata <- reactive(function() {
> >   # Don't do anything until after the first button push.
> >   if (input$recalcButton == 0)
> >     return(NULL)
> >
> >   # Note that just by virtue of checking the value of input$recalcButton,
> >   # we're now going to get called whenever it is pushed.
> >
> >   return(isolate({
> >     # Now do the expensive stuff
> >     foo <- activateInterlock(input$foo)
> >     bar <- connectDynotherm(input$bar)
> >     baz <- bringInfracellsUp(input$baz)
> >     c(foo=foo, bar=bar, baz=baz)
> >   }))
> > })
> >
> > So mydata will automatically react to changes in recalcButton (i.e. when it is pushed) but not to changes in the inputs foo, bar, or baz.
> >
> > How to install
> >
> > If you'd like to try isolate out for yourself, you can conveniently install the latest build from github using these commands:
> >
> > install.package("devtools")  # if necessary
> > devtools::install_github("shiny", "rstudio")
> >
> > (Glimmer users: We generally keep Glimmer synced to the version of Shiny that's on CRAN, so isolate probably won't be available there for at least a couple of weeks. Sorry.)

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I need some guidance, please. I have list of 12,000 gene symbols on the server side of my application. I wanted to provide my user with select2-type behavior whereby, as the user types a character, suggested symbols are presented in the selection list.

I tried the naive approach: I simply made the gene list the value of a select2 selection list. This works for around 500 symbols but does not work for 12,000 - there is no response from the server after several minutes. This behavior is understandable.

So, it seems that I might need an approach that employs a dialog between the ui and the server - narrowing down the list on the server side as the user types in characters. What I need some help with is the approach I should take. Should I use websockets or is there some combination of observe() and updateSelectInput that might work. I would like to retain the select2 functionality that allows the user to accumulate selections, that is, let the user select more than one gene symbol.

Thanks very much,

Peter

I had a similar issue, but my solution was a bit different- I created a search function of sorts, and then take their selection to use further.  This stuff was written before the shiny server had an updateUI function (I believe that is what is was called? maybe refreshUI? Oh well, in any event...)
### ui.R portion ###

checkboxInput("findGeneTopcheck", "Search for a Gene Symbol? (optional)"),
uiOutput("choose_geneTop1"),
uiOutput("choose_geneTop2")

### server.R portion ###
        output$choose_geneTop1 <- renderUI({
    conditionalPanel(
  condition = "input.findGeneTopcheck == true",
  textInput("findGeneTop", "Search for a Gene Symbol", "")
)

})
  output$choose_geneTop2 <- renderUI({

     if(is.null(tlist())) # tlist is a matrix that I wish to subset, eventually, and has the symbols in it
 return()
      if(is.null(topgeneinput()))
 return()
 tlist1=tlist()

    testl=unique(as.character(tlist1[,'sym'])) # get a vector of the gene symbols
    setsg=testl[grep(topgeneinput(),testl,ignore.case=TRUE)] # use grep to search and subset
    if(length(setsg)>500){ #if it's too big, take the first 500, they will be more specific if need be
    setsg=setsg[1:500]
    }
    #
    conditionalPanel( #make the UI
  condition = "input.findGeneTopcheck == true",
   selectInput("topselectedG", "Select the Gene Symbol",
              as.list(setsg))

)
})

Are you running Windows? If so, continue. If not, please reply to this e-mail telling us what OS you're using.
Exit all existing R sessions. This is important!
Start a fresh R session (I'm assuming you don't have httpuv or Shiny loaded on startup)
Run these R commands:
install.packages('httpuv', repos=c(RStudio='http://rstudio.org/_packages', CRAN='http://cran.rstudio.com'))
devtools::install_github('shiny', 'rstudio')
Try shiny::runExample('01_hello')
If that doesn't do the trick, please run sessionInfo() and reply with the results. Thanks and sorry for the inconvenience!
